newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. envoy Chretien says Zaire ceasefire a must.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy Chretien says Zaire ceasefire a must.

text.p: Raymond Chretien, the new U.N. envoy to Central Africa, said on Thursday he would focus on a ceasefire in Zaire before tackling any other problems in the growing crisis in the area.
Chretien, Canada's ambassador to Washington, is to leave shortly for the region, where fighting has dislodged more than 500,000 refugees from Rwanda and Burundi's civil wars.

Warfare between Zairean-born Tutsis, known as Banjamulenge, and other local tribes has led to an exodus of Rwandan Hutu refugees who fled to Zaire in the summer of 1994. Both the Zairean and Rwandan armies have entered the fray.

Chretien, who met Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on Thursday, said his first stop would be Lausanne, Switzerland where Zairean ruler Mobutu Sese Seko is secluded in a luxury hotel undergoing cancer treatment.
He also intends to speak to leaders of surrounding countries, especially Rwanda, as well as attempt to see to local leaders in eastern Zaire.
"A great urgency exists because of the fighting that is taking place in the region," he told reporters. "Only after a ceasefire will it be possible to tackle the humanitarian crisis.
"I will see whether the possibility for a dialogue exists. It is an extraordinary, complex situation but I will give it my best shot," he said.
Chretien, nephew of Canada's prime minister Jean Chretien, said he would insist on talking to the decision-makers and shuttle back and forth on an aircraft Canada has provided.
Although the United Nations has set up food camps in Rwanda for the Hutu refugees, few are going there, fearing revenge from the ruling Tutsis.

U.N spokeswoman Sylvana Foa said more than 6,000 Rwandan and Zairean refugees were spilling into Uganda. But only 1,300 Rwandans returned to their own country along with 4,500 Zaireans seeking shelter from the fighting.
She said food had been stockpiled on the Rwandan side of the border with Zaire and U.N. relief centres were ready to provide for about 15,000 people daiy.

Foa said aid workers were unable to reach more than half a million refugees in Uvira, Zaire, now controlled by the Banyamulenge Tutsis and in nearby Bukavu where she said the situation was now "completely out of control."

Meanwhile, Boutros-Ghali on Thursday again spoke to Mobuto by telephone in Lausanne as well as Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo in an effort to get more than 100 international aid workers from the United Nations and other groups out of Goma in eastern Zaire, Foa said.

Goma is the administrative centre for international relief operations to feed 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees in camps inside Zaire as well as an estimated 200,000 Burundians and thousands of Zaireans uprooted by nearly two weeks of fighting.
A pull-out by aid agencies would leave the refugees without any obvious means of support.

Mobutu, 66, has been in Switzerland since undergoing surgery for prostate cancer in August. His prolonged absence has raised fears about the future of his anarchic country if he dies. He is widely believed to have more than $4 billion in Swiss banks.

The Zairean leader, who seized power in 1965, has not made any public comment on the crisis and it is unclear if his tattered army can win back any territory lost to the Zairean Tutsis in the eastern part of the country.
